blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 16 (Lab Safety and Practical Skills (running header: Identifying Hazards and Designing Safe Experiments)), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.

blocks.prompt: 1 Why is a chemistry laboratory called a chemist workshop?
blocks.explanation: Because it is the place where a student is trained to observe the physical and chemical characteristics of substances by following definite procedures.

book_ref.quote: It is a place where a student is trained to observe the physical and chemical characteristics

blocks.prompt: 2 What should a student do before starting laboratory work?
blocks.explanation: He should get familiar with the layout of the laboratory and the fittings on the laboratory table and the side shelves, and determine the potential hazards of the equipment or experiment.

book_ref.quote: a student should get himself familiarized with the layout of the laboratory

blocks.prompt: 3 What dress precautions must be observed while working in the lab?
blocks.explanation: Always wear a lab coat and safety goggles. Girls must tie up their scarves and hair before starting work.

book_ref.quote: Girls must tie up their scarves and hair before start working in the lab.

blocks.prompt: 4 Why should students avoid crowding and stay at their own work places in the lab?
blocks.explanation: Crowding causes accidents. Students should stick to their work places at a safe distance from each other.

book_ref.quote: There must not be any crowding in the lab and students should stick to their work places

blocks.prompt: 5 Give two lab rules about food and testing of substances.
blocks.explanation: (i) No food items are brought into the lab. (ii) Never taste or smell any compound or gas.

book_ref.quote: Never taste or smell any compound or a gas.

blocks.text: 16.2 Common types of hazards in a laboratory

blocks.prompt: 6 Name the three categories of laboratory hazards.
blocks.explanation: Physical hazards, chemical hazards and biological hazards.

book_ref.quote: Most hazards which we might face while working in the laboratory fall into three categories

blocks.prompt: 7 Why should cut-resistant gloves be worn while handling broken glassware?
blocks.explanation: To prevent cuts, abrasions and skin damage. The broken glassware is then disposed of in a special container to prevent injury.

book_ref.quote: to prevent cuts, abrasions and skin damage

blocks.prompt: 8 Differentiate between physical hazards and biological hazards.
blocks.explanation: Physical hazards are accidents such as slipping and falling; biological hazards come from living sources such as allergens and infections.

book_ref.quote: The most common physical hazards are slips and falls when working on wet floor.

rows: Most common: slips and falls when working on a wet floor.
Most common: allergens, infectious diseases transferred from animals to humans, and viral diseases.
Also cuts and abrasions from broken glassware.
Arise from living sources (animals, viruses).
Prevented by care, cut-resistant gloves and a special container for broken glass.
Need protection from allergens and infections.

blocks.prompt: 9 How can chemical hazards be reduced in a laboratory?
blocks.explanation: By using every chemical according to the standard procedures, keeping in view its particular hazards (shown by hazard pictograms) and the precautions needed for its safe use.

book_ref.quote: keeping in view the particular hazards and precautions required for the safe use

blocks.prompt: 10 Name three common biological hazards of a laboratory.
blocks.explanation: (i) Allergens (ii) infectious diseases transferred from animals to humans (iii) viral diseases.

book_ref.quote: Figure 16.3: Some biological hazards

blocks.prompt: 11 Why can chemical waste not be thrown into bins or the sewer?
blocks.explanation: Chemical waste must be disposed of under the rules and regulations of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA): it is stored in proper labelled containers and treated at an allocated site, not thrown into bins or the sewer.

book_ref.quote: Most chemical wastes must be disposed of keeping in view the following rules and regulation

blocks.prompt: 12 What information should be written on the label of a chemical waste container?
blocks.explanation: The types of wastes, the date of the waste and the place of origin.

book_ref.quote: Store chemical wastes in proper containers.

blocks.prompt: 13 Name four methods of chemical treatment of wastes.
blocks.explanation: Neutralization, precipitation, ion exchange, and oxidation or reduction.

book_ref.quote: where these are appropriately treated to dispose them off

blocks.prompt: 14 What first aid is given for (i) a minor cut and (ii) a serious cut?
blocks.explanation: (i) Minor cut: remove any glass piece, apply a little methylated spirit or tincture iodine with cotton (both act as disinfectant). (ii) Serious cut: apply pressure on the cut for about 10 minutes to stop bleeding and consult a doctor.

book_ref.quote: Every laboratory must have a first aid box.

blocks.prompt: 15 Why are methylated spirit and tincture iodine applied to a minor cut?
blocks.explanation: Both act as disinfectants, so they protect the cut from infection.

book_ref.quote: Both act as disinfectant.

blocks.prompt: 16 Differentiate between the first aid for acid in the eye and alkali in the eye.
blocks.explanation: Both are first washed with water; the acid is then neutralised with a weak base and the alkali with a weak acid.

book_ref.quote: Wash thoroughly with water and then with 1% sodium bicarbonate solution.

rows: Wash thoroughly with water.
Wash with water.
Then wash with 1% sodium bicarbonate solution.
Then wash with 1% boric acid solution.
Sodium bicarbonate is a weak base.
Boric acid is a weak acid.

blocks.prompt: 17 What should be done if a foreign particle gets into the eye?
blocks.explanation: Do not rub the eyes. Remove the particle carefully with a soft handkerchief, then wash with water.

book_ref.quote: Foreign particle in the eye

blocks.prompt: 18 Differentiate between the first aid for an acid burn and an alkali burn.
blocks.explanation: An acid burn is neutralised with a weak base, an alkali burn with a weak acid.

book_ref.quote: Table 16.1 lists five kinds of burns but prints only four treatments

rows: Wash with ice cold water.
Wash freely with water.
Then wash with saturated sodium bicarbonate solution (weak base).
Then wash with 1% acetic acid solution (weak acid).
Wash again with water.
Wash again with water, dry the skin and apply burnol.

blocks.prompt: 19 What is the first aid for (i) a burn by dry heat and (ii) a bromine burn?
blocks.explanation: (i) Dry heat (flame, hot object): apply burnol or mustard oil. (ii) Bromine burn: wash with 2% ammonia solution and apply glycerin; wipe off the glycerin after some time and apply burnol.

book_ref.quote: Burns with dry heat (flame, hot object)

blocks.prompt: 20 Differentiate between the first aid when an acid is swallowed and when a caustic alkali is swallowed.
blocks.explanation: In both cases drink a lot of water; then a base neutralises the acid and a fruit juice (acid) neutralises the alkali.

book_ref.quote: Caustic alkalies swallowed

rows: Drink a lot of water.
Drink a lot of water.
Or drink lime water or milk of magnesia.
Then drink a glass of lemon or orange juice.

blocks.prompt: 21 What first aid is given when (i) a poison or (ii) a salt of a heavy metal is swallowed?
blocks.explanation: (i) Poison swallowed: spit immediately and wash the mouth with water repeatedly. (ii) Salt of a heavy metal: take milk or the white part of an egg.

book_ref.quote: Salt of heavy metals swallowed.

blocks.prompt: 22 Why should water not be thrown on burning spirit or oil? What should be used instead?
blocks.explanation: Water will simply spread the fire. Throw a mixture of sand and sodium bicarbonate instead.

book_ref.quote: Do not throw water. It will simply spread the fire.

blocks.prompt: 23 How is a fire in electric parts dealt with?
blocks.explanation: Switch off the electric supply immediately and throw sand. Water must not be thrown to extinguish such a fire.

book_ref.quote: Do not throw water in such cases to extinguish fire.

blocks.prompt: 24 Why does covering a burning beaker of inflammable liquid with a damp cloth put out the fire?
blocks.explanation: The duster or damp cloth cuts off the supply of oxygen, and without oxygen the liquid cannot keep burning.

book_ref.quote: This will cut off the supply of oxygen.

blocks.prompt: 25 What should a person do if his clothes catch fire?
blocks.explanation: Do not run. Wrap yourself in a blanket or dry cotton cloth and lie down on the floor.

book_ref.quote: Wrap with blanket or with dry cotton cloth.

blocks.prompt: 26 What is volumetric analysis?
blocks.explanation: Volumetric analysis finds the concentrations of solutions by titration: a solution of unknown concentration is combined slowly and carefully with a known volume of a standard solution until a colour change shows the reaction is complete.

book_ref.quote: In this technique a solution of unknown concentration is combined slowly and carefully

blocks.prompt: 27 Differentiate between an indicator and the end point.
blocks.explanation: The indicator is a substance; the end point is a moment in the titration.

book_ref.quote: until a colour change shows the completion of the reaction

rows: A substance which shows the completion of reaction by a change in its colour.
The moment at which the indicator changes colour.
Example: phenolphthalein.
Example: the pink colour just disappears in the HCl-NaOH titration.
Added (one to two drops) before the titration.
Reached during the titration; the burette reading is then taken.

blocks.prompt: 28 How is phenolphthalein indicator solution prepared, and how much is used?
blocks.explanation: One gram of the indicator is added to 500 cm³ of 50% ethanol. Only one to two drops are used in 10 cm³ of the solution to be titrated.

book_ref.quote: Use only one to two drops in 10 cm³ of the solution to be titrated.

blocks.prompt: 29 Why does the light pink colour of phenolphthalein at the end point fade gradually?
blocks.explanation: Atmospheric carbon dioxide slowly dissolves in the solution and interferes; the pH decreases and phenolphthalein turns from pink towards colourless.

book_ref.quote: which slowly dissolves in the solution

blocks.prompt: 30 Why is the funnel removed from the burette after filling, and why is a little acid run out into a beaker?
blocks.explanation: The funnel is removed after filling the burette with HCl. Some acid is run into a beaker through the tap to remove any air bubble in the nozzle before the initial reading is noted.

book_ref.quote: Fix the burette on a clamp stand in an upright position.

blocks.prompt: 31 Why is the conical flask swirled during the titration?
blocks.explanation: Swirling while adding the acid gives thorough mixing, so the colour change of the indicator appears exactly at the end point.

book_ref.quote: The contents of the flask must be swirled adding of acid for thorough mixing.

blocks.prompt: 32 What are concordant readings?
blocks.explanation: Titration readings that agree with one another within 0.1 cm³. At least three concordant readings are taken to get an accurate result.

book_ref.quote: Repeat the titration to get accurate and concordant readings.

blocks.prompt: 33 In the HCl-NaOH titration with phenolphthalein, what colour change marks the end point? Give a reason.
blocks.explanation: Pink to colourless. NaOH with phenolphthalein in the flask is pink; acid from the burette lowers the pH, and the pink colour just disappears at the end point.

book_ref.quote: Check that the burette does not leak.

blocks.prompt: 34 The initial burette reading is 0.40 cm³ and the final reading is 13.15 cm³. Find the volume of HCl used.
blocks.explanation: Volume used = final − initial = 13.15 − 0.40 = 12.75 cm³.

book_ref.quote: Volume of HCl solution used = ________ cm³

blocks.prompt: 35 Write the molarity equation used in acid-base titration and explain its symbols.
blocks.explanation: M₁V₁/n₁ (acid) = M₂V₂/n₂ (base). M₁, V₁ = molarity and volume of acid; M₂, V₂ = molarity and volume of base; n₁, n₂ = moles of acid and base in the balanced equation. So M₂ = (M₁V₁/n₁) × (n₂/V₂).

book_ref.quote: Molarity of the given base solution is ____ M.

blocks.prompt: 36 10 cm³ of NaOH solution is neutralised by 8.0 cm³ of 0.25 M HCl. Find the molarity of the NaOH solution.
blocks.explanation: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O, so n₁ = n₂ = 1. M₂ = M₁V₁/V₂ = 0.25 × 8.0 / 10 = 0.20 M.

book_ref.quote: M₂ = Molarity of base solution

blocks.prompt: 37 How is the carbonate radical identified? Give the equations.
blocks.explanation: Add dilute HCl to the solid: brisk effervescence; the gas turns lime water milky. CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂; Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ (white ppt) + H₂O.

book_ref.quote: Take about 2 g of solid carbonate sample in a clean test tube

blocks.prompt: 38 Why is the salt solution acidified with dilute HNO₃ before adding AgNO₃ in the halide tests?
blocks.explanation: Dilute nitric acid prevents carbonate ions from precipitating along with the halide ions, so the precipitate formed is due to the halide only.

book_ref.quote: In the above tests for the detection of halide ions

blocks.prompt: 39 Differentiate between the chloride and iodide tests with acidified AgNO₃.
blocks.explanation: Both give a silver halide precipitate, but the colour differs.

book_ref.quote: Identification of chloride, bromide and iodide radicals

rows: Thick white precipitate.
Bright yellow precipitate.
Precipitate dissolves in aqueous NH₃.
Not described as dissolving in NH₃.
Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl(s)
Ag⁺ + I⁻ → AgI(s)

blocks.prompt: 40 How is the bromide ion identified? Write the equation.
blocks.explanation: Dissolve the salt in water, acidify with dilute HNO₃ and add aqueous AgNO₃: a thick cream-yellow precipitate shows Br¹⁻. Ag⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq) → AgBr(s).

book_ref.quote: A thick cream-yellow precipitate is formed.

blocks.prompt: 41 What is the role of aluminium in the test for nitrate ions?
blocks.explanation: Aluminium is the reducing agent: it is oxidised to [Al(OH)₄]¹⁻ and reduces NO₃¹⁻ to ammonia gas in NaOH solution. (No cell is involved, so it is not a cathode.)

book_ref.quote: The reduction of NO₃¹⁻ with aluminium metal is a redox reaction

blocks.prompt: 42 How is the gas evolved in the nitrate test identified?
blocks.explanation: It is NH₃: it has a characteristic smell near the mouth of the test tube and turns red litmus paper blue.

book_ref.quote: This gas turns red litmus paper blue.

blocks.prompt: 43 How is the sulphate radical identified? Write the equation.
blocks.explanation: Dissolve the salt in water, acidify with dilute HNO₃ and add barium nitrate solution: a heavy white precipitate of BaSO₄ shows SO₄²⁻. SO₄²⁻(aq) + Ba²⁺(aq) → BaSO₄(s).

book_ref.quote: then add 5 cm³ barium nitrate solution

blocks.text: 16.7 Tests for identification of basic radicals

blocks.prompt: 44 How is the Al³⁺ radical identified? Write the equation.
blocks.explanation: With NaOH solution a white gelatinous precipitate forms; with a few drops of aqueous ammonia a white precipitate forms. Al³⁺ + 3OH¹⁻ → Al(OH)₃(s) (white ppt).

book_ref.quote: To the second part of the above solution, add a few drops of aqueous ammonia.

blocks.prompt: 45 How is the ammonium radical identified? Write the equation.
blocks.explanation: Warm the salt solution gently with NaOH: ammonia gas with a distinct smell is given off, which turns moist red litmus blue. NH₄¹⁺ + OH¹⁻ → NH₃(g) + H₂O(l).

book_ref.quote: Ammonia gas is evolved with a distinct smell.

blocks.prompt: 46 Differentiate between the reactions of Cr³⁺ and Cu²⁺ ions with NaOH and aqueous ammonia.
blocks.explanation: Cr³⁺ gives green products; Cu²⁺ gives blue ones.

book_ref.quote: Identification of chromium radical

rows: NaOH: green precipitate of Cr(OH)₃, which turns into a green solution in excess NaOH.
NaOH: light-blue precipitate of Cu(OH)₂.
Aqueous ammonia: green precipitate, insoluble in excess ammonia.
Aqueous ammonia: deep blue solution.

blocks.prompt: 47 Write the equation for the reaction of Cu²⁺ ions with NaOH solution and name the colour of the product.
blocks.explanation: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s). The precipitate of Cu(OH)₂ is light blue.

book_ref.quote: Copper(II) ions with a small amount and an excess of ammonia

blocks.prompt: 48 What is observed when NaOH solution is added to FeCl₃ solution? Write the equation.
blocks.explanation: An orange brown precipitate of Fe(OH)₃ forms, showing Fe³⁺. Fe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s).

book_ref.quote: Make two portions of the solution for further tests.

blocks.prompt: 49 How do Zn²⁺ ions behave with aqueous ammonia, first in small amount and then in excess?
blocks.explanation: A white precipitate of Zn(OH)₂ forms first, and it dissolves in excess of ammonia.

book_ref.quote: To second portion of the above solution add aqueous ammonia.
